chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Abdullah ibn Bahr, from Abdullah ibn Muskan, from Abu Basir who said:
I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): [What is the meaning of] the word of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, in His Book:
'And do not consume your property among yourselves by false means, and present it to the judges'

So he said: O Abu Basir! Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has known that in the community there are judges who are tyrannous. Indeed, He did not mean the judges of the people of justice, but He meant the judges of the people of tyranny.

O Abu Muhammad! If there were a right for you against a man, and you summoned him to the judges of the people of justice, but he refused you unless you took the matter to the judges of the people of tyranny so that they judge in his favor — he would be among those who sought judgment from the taghut.
And this is the word of Allah, Mighty and Majestic:
'Have you not seen those who allege that they believe in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you? They desire to seek judgment from the taghut.'

key_terms.الطاغوت: Taghut — the tyrant or false authority to whom judgment is improperly referred; used in the Quran to describe any authority that opposes divine law
key_terms.حكام أهل الجور: Judges of the people of tyranny — unjust rulers appointed without divine sanction
key_terms.حكام أهل العدل: Judges of the people of justice — legitimate, divinely-sanctioned authorities
key_terms.يجورون: They commit injustice/tyranny — those who deviate from justice in their rulings

ai.seo_question: What did Imam al-Sadiq say about seeking judgment from unjust judges in Islam?
ai.summary: Abu Basir asks Imam al-Sadiq (AS) about the Quranic verse (2:188) prohibiting consumption of property through false means and submitting disputes to judges. The Imam clarifies that the prohibition specifically targets unjust judges (the taghut), not just rulers. He illustrates this with a legal scenario: if a person refuses to appear before a just judge and instead insists on taking matters to a tyrannical court to gain an unfair advantage, that person has effectively worshipped the taghut — as condemned in Quran 4:60. This hadith was addressed to a close companion in the context of Shia jurisprudence under Abbasid rule, where seeking redress from government-appointed (unjust) judges was a live dilemma.
